about: In what order every SCE engine writes the members of a JSON object into
`_event.data`, written out by hand.
One order: ascending by the key's UTF-8 bytes, which is ascending by
Unicode code point, at every depth. RFC 8259 leaves the order of an
object's members open and SCE closes it, so the same `<send>` is the same
bytes whichever engine wrote it - and a machine's saved state, which holds
a host request's `event_data` as text, reads the same on every backend.
Why a shared table: measured 2026-10-02, the Kotlin writer kept the order
a document declared its `<param>`s in while the C++, Rust, Go and Python
writers sorted them, and nothing pinned either. A document that declared
`b` before `a` produced `{"b":..,"a":..}` on one backend and
`{"a":..,"b":..}` on the rest, and a state saved on one could not be
compared byte for byte with a state saved on another.
Each case gives `params`, what a `<send>` evaluated, as [name, value]
pairs in the order the document declared them (a value is any JSON value),
and `data`, the exact `_event.data` text the writer must produce. A name
that repeats collects its values, in document order, into one array
(W3C SCXML test178: an object cannot hold a name twice). A number is a
whole number, so the cases do not depend on how an engine spells a
fraction. The rule is stated once, in ARCHITECTURE.md, 'JSON Object Key
Order', which lists the readers.

cases.name: declaration order is not the written order
upper case sorts before lower case
digits sort as text, not as numbers
a prefix sorts before what extends it
a supplementary character sorts after every character of the basic plane
a name that repeats is one array in declaration order
an object value is ordered at every depth
digits sort as text inside an object value too
an object inside an array is ordered and the array is not
a string value is written in the one escape form
